calls.head: Who drives the play: the Senators
calls.body: The Senators have been near the top of the league at controlling the chances at 5-on-5, and the Islanders around the middle. Expect the Senators to spend more of the night in the Islanders’ end. That’s about the puck, not the scoreboard: goalies and finishing decide plenty of games the chances don’t.
calls.call: The Senators get the bigger share of the 5-on-5 chances.

calls.head: Depth vs. Star power
calls.body: On depth, the Islanders are one of the league’s best, but Ottawa is one of the worst. They’re about as far apart as two teams get. If this one comes down to the bottom six, that suits the Islanders.
calls.call: The Islanders spread their forward ice time deeper down the lineup than the Senators.

surprises.head: The Islanders’ power play hit a new low
surprises.body: The Islanders have had one of the league’s least effective power plays for years. Even by those standards, this was a dry night: 2.1 expected goals per 60 on the power play, against their usual 7.2 (about 6.6 against Ottawa) and a league average of 7.6. A team strays this far about once every 15 games.

story.head: Pinto seals it in the shootout
paras: Ottawa had a goal taken off for offside midway through the first, though it didn’t end up costing them. Matias Maccelli got the scoring started for the Islanders with 12 seconds left in the first, but Ridly Greig made it 1-1 for Ottawa late in the second. Shane Pinto scored the only goal of the shootout for the Senators. Artem Zub played his first game of the season, after missing the first seven, and picked up an assist.

The Senators owned the chances, and still had to sweat it out in a shootout. Linus Ullmark made 20 saves for the Sens, and Semyon Varlamov kept the Islanders in it, stopping 18 of 19. Ullmark has won all six of his starts this season. The Senators moved to 6-2-0 and climbed into first in the Atlantic, while the Islanders fell to 3-3-1, fifth in the Metropolitan.
